title: The information capacity of the human motor system in controlling the amplitude of movement
authority: Paul Fitts was an experimental psychologist and founder of the US Air Force aviation psychology program; this is the origin of Fitts' law.
caveats: Original tasks were reciprocal tapping and disc transfer with a stylus; later work (Welford, Shannon formulation by MacKenzie) revised the index of difficulty. Does not model steering, 2D area targets or touch finger occlusion well without adaptation.

title: On the rate of gain of information
authority: William Edmund Hick, Cambridge Applied Psychology Unit; first showed choice reaction time grows with the information content of the choice.
caveats: Tested up to 10 alternatives with highly practiced participants and equiprobable stimuli; the law fails with high stimulus-response compatibility, heavy practice, and very large or unordered sets. Frequently misapplied to menu and page design.

title: Stimulus information as a determinant of reaction time
authority: Ray Hyman, experimental psychologist; independently confirmed Hick's result and extended it to unequal probabilities and sequential dependencies.
caveats: Laboratory choice reaction tasks with small stimulus sets; does not directly license claims about visual menu scanning.

title: Hick's law for choice reaction time: A review
authority: Proctor is a leading researcher on stimulus-response compatibility; the review is the standard modern assessment of Hick's law and its limits.
caveats: Review of the laboratory literature; HCI applications are discussed briefly.

title: Fitts' law as a research and design tool in human-computer interaction
authority: MacKenzie is the leading authority on Fitts' law in HCI; this paper established the Shannon formulation and method guidance later adopted in ISO 9241-411.
caveats: Mouse and stylus era; touch needs adjustments (see Bi2013FFitts).

title: Evaluation of mouse, rate-controlled isometric joystick, step keys, and text keys for text selection on a CRT
authority: Xerox PARC study that demonstrated the mouse outperformed alternatives and showed that its pointing followed Fitts' law.
caveats: Small sample, 1970s devices; the Fitts' law constants are device specific.

title: The keystroke-level model for user performance time with interactive systems
authority: Card, Moran and Newell founded cognitive engineering of HCI; KLM is the simplest GOMS family model.
caveats: Predicts only error-free expert execution time; ignores learning, errors and thinking beyond a heuristic M operator. Operator times are from desktop keyboards and mice.

title: The Psychology of Human-Computer Interaction
authority: The founding text of cognitive modelling in HCI; introduces the Model Human Processor and GOMS.
caveats: Serial, expert, error-free model; criticized as unsuited to exploratory or learning behavior and to situated action.

title: The magical number seven, plus or minus two: Some limits on our capacity for processing information
authority: Miller was a founder of cognitive psychology; the paper introduced chunking as a way to extend memory span.
caveats: Miller himself treated seven as a rough rhetorical pattern. Widely misused to cap menu items or navigation links; Cowan2001 revises capacity to about four chunks.

title: The magical number 4 in short-term memory: A reconsideration of mental storage capacity
authority: Cowan is a leading working-memory researcher; the target article was published with open peer commentary.
caveats: Capacity estimates remain debated (slot versus resource models, Ma, Husain and Bays 2014); the 3 to 5 chunk figure applies when rehearsal and chunking are prevented.

title: Beyond Fitts' law: Models for trajectory-based HCI tasks
authority: Zhai is a leading HCI input researcher; the paper derives the steering law for moving through constrained paths.
caveats: Lab tunnel tasks; real menus and sliders have looser constraints, and speed-accuracy tradeoffs differ across devices.

title: Mechanisms of skill acquisition and the law of practice
authority: Newell was a founder of cognitive science; the chapter documents that performance time follows a power function of practice across many domains.
caveats: Heathcote, Brown and Mewhort (2000) argued exponential functions fit individual learners better than power functions; averaging across participants can create a spurious power law. Some records list pages 1-51; check the printed volume.

title: Direct manipulation: A step beyond programming languages
authority: Shneiderman coined the term direct manipulation and founded the University of Maryland HCI Lab.
caveats: Conceptual and anecdotal rather than experimental; direct manipulation has known limits for abstraction and repetitive tasks.

title: Direct manipulation interfaces
authority: Cognitive scientists who analyzed why direct manipulation feels direct, through the gulfs of execution and evaluation.
caveats: Theoretical analysis; the notion of directness is not operationalized into measurable criteria.

title: As we may think
authority: Bush directed US wartime scientific research; the essay envisioned the Memex and associative trails, inspiring hypertext.
caveats: A vision, not an empirical study; technical details (microfilm) are obsolete. One secondary index gives different page numbers; 101-108 is the commonly cited range.

title: Man-computer symbiosis
container: IRE Transactions on Human Factors in Electronics
authority: Licklider was a psychologist and ARPA program director who shaped interactive computing.
caveats: A forecast; its prediction of interactive partnership has largely come true but the timescale was optimistic.

title: Information theoretic models of HCI: A comparison of the Hick-Hyman law and Fitts' law
authority: Peer-reviewed comparative treatment of the two main information-theoretic laws, with guidance on how to apply them.
caveats: Theoretical review; empirical use of the laws in design still needs task-specific calibration. Journal volume and pages could not be confirmed by search this session; DOI unconfirmed.

title: Information capacity of discrete motor responses
authority: Follow-up by Fitts that tested the law with discrete (single) aimed movements, the form closest to a button press.
caveats: Throughput figures quoted from a secondary source (about 13.5 bits/s discrete); check the original table before quoting.

title: How relevant is Hick's law for HCI?
authority: Peer-reviewed CHI paper by HCI and information-theory researchers that tests how far Hick's law applies to interface design.
caveats: Argues against the common reading that fewer choices is always faster; full empirical details not read this session.

title: FFitts law: Modeling finger touch with Fitts' law
authority: Google Research and Stony Brook authors; the main model for finger touch endpoint variability.
caveats: A 2021 follow-up reports FFitts did not always fit better than Fitts' law with nominal width, so its advantage is not uniformly replicated.
